p.src: I owed this kappa named Lap no less than I did Bag for all the help he gave me. But the most unforgettable thing he did was introduce me to a kappa named Tock. Tock was a poet among the kappas. Poets there wore their hair long, just as they do among us humans. From time to time, I visited Tock at home to relieve my boredom. Tock kept pots of alpine plants lined up in his cramped room and lived a thoroughly carefree life, writing poetry and smoking tobacco. In one corner of that room there was also a female kappa—Tock was an advocate of free love, so he had no such thing as a wife— knitting or doing something of the sort. Whenever Tock saw me, he would smile and say: (Though a kappa's smile is not a particularly pleasant sight. At least at first, I found it rather uncanny.) “Ah, good of you to come. Come, sit down in that chair.” Tock often talked about the life of the kappas and the art of the kappas. In Tock's view, nothing was more absurd than the ordinary life of an ordinary kappa. Parents and children, husbands and wives, brothers and sisters—all of them lived as though their sole pleasure were tormenting one another. The institution of the family in particular was absurd beyond absurdity. Once, Tock pointed out of the window and said, “Look. Just look at that absurdity!” He spat out the words. In the street outside the window, a still-young kappa was staggering along, scarcely able to breathe, with seven or eight male and female kappas—including what appeared to be his parents—hanging around his neck. But I was impressed by the young kappa's spirit of self-sacrifice, and instead praised his admirable devotion to the skies. “Hmph. You are qualified to become a citizen even in this country.

p.src: Naturally, I replied, “Qua” (which in the language of the kappas means “Yes”). That was my answer. “Then you would surely have no qualms about sacrificing one genius for the sake of a hundred ordinary fools.” “Then what sort of ‘ist’ are you? Someone told me that your creed was anarchism, Tock...” “Me? I am a superman—literally, a super-kappa— that's what I am.” Tock declared this with magnificent pride. Tock also held distinctive ideas about art. According to Tock, art submits to the rule of nothing; it is art for art's sake, and therefore an artist must first and foremost be a superman who has transcended good and evil. This, however, was not necessarily Tock's opinion alone. Most of the poets in Tock's circle seemed to share it. Indeed, I often went with Tock to visit the Superman Club. Those who gathered at the Superman Club included poets, novelists, playwrights, critics, painters, musicians, sculptors, and artistic amateurs. But every one of them was a superman. They were always conversing cheerfully in a brightly lit salon. What was more, they would sometimes proudly demonstrate to one another just how superhuman they were. One sculptor, for example, would seize a young kappa among the pots of great tree ferns and eagerly indulge in sodomy. And one female novelist stood atop a table and proceeded to drink sixty bottles of absinthe for all to see. Though the moment she finished the sixtieth bottle and tumbled beneath the table, she promptly expired. One moonlit evening, I came home from the Superman Club arm in arm with Tock the poet.

p.src: Tock was unusually dejected and did not utter a word. Presently we passed a small window glowing with firelight. Beyond it, two kappas, a male and a female who appeared to be husband and wife, were seated at the dinner table with their three kappa children. Then Tock sighed and suddenly spoke to me.

u.src: Tock was unusually dejected and did not utter a word.
Presently we passed a small window glowing with firelight.
Beyond it, two kappas, a male and a female who appeared to be husband and wife, were seated at the dinner table with their three kappa children.
Then Tock sighed and suddenly spoke to me.

p.src: “I consider myself a superhuman lover, you know, but when I see a family like that, I still can’t help feeling envious.” “But however you look at it, don’t you think that’s a contradiction?” But Tock remained motionless in the moonlight with his arms folded, gazing through that little window—at the peaceful supper table of the five kappas. After a while, he answered: “After all, the omelet over there is more wholesome than any love affair.”
